newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus passes 1997 budget, economists not cheered.
newsitem.headline: Belarus passes 1997 budget, economists not cheered.

text.p: Belarus passed its 1997 budget on Friday and economists welcomed the move but said much work remained to be done to get the economy on its feet.

Prime Minister Sergei Ling told the upper house of parliament, which approved a law setting a deficit of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product from 1.9 percent last year, that the economy would improve dramatically this year.
"Practically all parameters of growth should double in our economy in 1997. Positive signs in 1996 give grounds for optimism," he said.

World Bank representative Christopher Willoughby later told a news conference he welcomed the passing of the budget but added: "Fundamental issues concerning the future development of the economy remain to solved".

Nikolai Lisai, an advisor to the bank, painted a bleaker picture, saying: "The budget cannot be looked at optimistically. Exports and profitability in industry and the agrarian sector are continuing to fall, while inflation and non-payment of credits are continuing to grow".
International lending organisations like the bank and the International Monetary Fund have suspended credits to the former Soviet republic of 10 million pending faster reforms.
President Alexander Lukashenko keeps a tight rein on the Belarussian rouble currency, on banks and on prices.
The budget foresees a five-percent growth in gross domestic product against a 2.6 percent rise last year, while industrial growth is to improve by six percent against 3.2 percent.
Economists are sceptical about the significance of last year's GDP growth, saying it is unsustainable as some of it came from sales of low-quality goods to poorer regions of neighbouring Russia.
Revised figures were not read out for revenue, previously set at 35 trillion Belarussian roubles, and expenditure, which had been set at 43 trillion Belarussian roubles.
But Russia's Interfax news agency said the new figures were 36.6 trillion and 44.05 trillion Belarussian roubles respectively.
Average monthly inflation is forecast at two percent against 3.6 percent last year.
